nameStory: Gonatozygon brebissonii doesn't have a widely-used common name since it's a microscopic freshwater alga that most people never see without a microscope. The scientific name honors Alphonse de Brébisson, a 19th-century French botanist who specialized in studying these tiny water plants. If we had to give it a common name, 'knee-joint algae' would fit, since 'gonato' means knee-like and refers to the bent shape of its cells.
description: This is a single-celled freshwater alga so small you'd need a microscope to see it clearly - each cell is only about the width of a human hair. Unlike the green plants we usually think of, this tiny organism lives floating in ponds, lakes, and slow streams throughout New England. It's part of a group called conjugating green algae, which means it reproduces by joining with other cells. You might encounter it as part of the greenish film or scum that sometimes appears on quiet water surfaces.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are invisible to the naked eye, requiring at least 100x magnification to observe clearly - about 20-40 micrometers long

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Cells appear elongated and slightly curved or bent, like a tiny green banana under the microscope

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in still or slow-moving freshwater - look for greenish films on pond surfaces or quiet stream backwaters

idTips.label: Color appearance
idTips.description: Contributes to bright green coloration in water, often with a slightly slimy or filmy texture when present in large numbers

habitat: Lives in quiet freshwater environments throughout New England, including ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and temporary pools. Prefers nutrient-rich water and can be found from sea level to mountain elevations. Often occurs alongside other microscopic algae in the surface films of still water bodies.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms, contributing to early season algae blooms in ponds and lakes.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when you're most likely to notice green films on water surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as temperatures drop, though some populations persist in warmer micro-environments.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant in most New England waters, surviving as resistant stages until spring warming.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, this single-celled organism can reproduce by literally reaching out and connecting with another cell to exchange genetic material - like microscopic handshaking that creates the next generation!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other microscopic green algae in water samples, but requires expert identification under high magnification. To most observers, it's simply part of the general 'pond scum' that includes many different microscopic species.
contextualKnowledge: This represents the hidden world of microscopic life that most nature explorers never see, yet these tiny organisms form the foundation of freshwater food webs. What we casually call 'pond scum' is actually a complex community of dozens of different microscopic species.
compareHints: Differs from its relatives Gonatozygon kinahanii by its specific cell dimensions and shape details visible only under high magnification. Unlike Gonatozygon aculeatum, it lacks spiny projections on the cell surface. All species in this genus require expert microscopic examination to distinguish reliably from one another.
